title: To whom did this thought come?
hookLine: a silent young swami on Arunachala writes out his answers for a visitor
carry: trace each thought back to the self
tomorrow: karma: the king who gave away his last meal
last: GOD SEARCHES FOR THE SOUL TOO.

lines: A SILENT SWAMI WRITES HIS ANSWERS.
cards: Around 1902, a visitor named Sivaprakasam Pillai climbs the hill of Arunachala to a cave where a young swami lives. That's Ramana, still in his early twenties.

Pillai has brought a list of questions, but in those years Ramana hardly speaks. So he answers in writing. The first question on the list is the one Ramana asked himself at sixteen, on that floor: who am I?
Pillai keeps the answers, and they become a small book, Nan Yar?, Who Am I? One of its moves is about what happens the second any of us sits still: a thought shows up.

teach.h: TO WHOM DID THIS THOUGHT COME? TO ME.
teach.b: Your mind plans dinner. Then it replays something someone said on Tuesday. Most advice gives two options: fight the thought, or follow it.
Don't chase it, and don't wrestle it. Ask: to whom did this thought come? The answer comes back instantly: to me.

Then ask: and who am I? In that moment the attention turns around. Instead of flowing out toward dinner or Tuesday, it flows back toward its own source, and the thought drops away, because nobody's feeding it.
His reasoning: of all thoughts, the thought I is the first. Every other thought is a thought to someone: I'm hungry, I'm annoyed, I remember. Trace I back, and every other thought loses its root.
Ramana called this atma-vichara, inquiry into the Self: the same atman the boy found on the floor. He gave a picture from the cremation ground.

teach.h: THE STICK THAT STIRS THE FIRE BURNS TOO.
teach.b: A stick stirs the cremation fire, and at the end the stick itself is thrown into the flames.
The question who am I works like that stick: it burns away the other thoughts, and in the end it burns away too, leaving only what was there all along.
Ramana was generous about other roads. If you can't inquire, he said, surrender completely to God; both lead to the same place. And it's portable: no temple, no book.
The next time a thought won't let you sleep, one question.

how: People who follow Ramana Maharshi's teaching practice self-inquiry in daily life and in silent sitting, turning each thought back with the question 'to whom?'; many combine it with devotion, as Ramana allowed.

o: fighting each thought until the mind is clear
action, even one question turned back inward
following each thought to see where it goes

burned in the fire at the end

s: Ramana taught people to fight their thoughts until the mind is empty

games.q: you're sitting quietly and a thought about dinner arrives. what does Ramana suggest?
o: ask: to whom did this thought come? and who am I?
games.why: don't fight, don't follow: ask to whom. the attention turns back toward its source, and the thought loses its root.

practice: Let thoughts come as they will, and when one appears, don't push it away or follow it; ask quietly: to whom did this come? To me. And who am I?
Let the attention rest wherever it lands, without needing an answer, and ask again with the next thought; ten times in two minutes is the practice working.
If surrender suits you better, as Ramana allowed, you can simply hand each thought to God instead.

wordCard.voice: Karma, action, is the word these weeks carry. Ramana's action is the smallest one on the path: one question, turned back toward the one who asks.

orig.note: Sanskrit: atma-vichara, inquiry (vichara) into the self (atma); Ramana's name for his method, atma-vicharam in Tamil.

carryVoice: Your line: trace each thought back to the Self. One question does it: to whom? Day three hundred nineteen, done.

sources.ref: Ramana Maharshi, Nan Yar? (Who Am I?), his answers to Sivaprakasam Pillai at Arunachala (c. 1902): 'to whom did this thought arise?'; the I-thought as root; the stick stirring the pyre; surrender as an alternative
